text: Drones, texts, and diversions: how Mexico captured a most wanted man. When Mexican soldiers arrived in trucks at the house holding one of Mexico’s most wanted drug lords, they encountered heavy gunfire. The soldiers, part of an elite special forces unit, returned fire and stormed toward their target. They seized Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, who US authorities say led a criminal group that trafficked vast quantities of drugs to the United States and fueled years of bloodshed in Mexico. After at least two failed attempts by Mexican authorities over the years, they finally had handcuffs on Meza Flores, one of a string of top cartel bosses that Mexico, with help from the United States, has captured or killed. In this case, Meza Flores had landed on the FBI’s most-wanted fugitive list, accused of leading a syndicate that has used violence and intimidation to build a criminal empire spanning dozens of countries, funneling staggering quantities of fentanyl, methamphetamine, and cocaine into the United States and worldwide. Whether his arrest puts a dent in the drug trade remains to be seen, but taking down such a major figure was a significant victory. Authorities’ next problem was getting him out of Sinaloa, the Mexican state in the depths of a chaotic cartel war. The operation began around 4 p.m. Friday, after weeks of collaboration between the Mexican military and US intelligence officials, according to officials familiar with the raid’s details who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss them candidly. As the raid unfolded, residents recorded footage of army helicopters, flaming cars, and firefights in the streets. And in the operation’s aftermath, US officials revealed that they had assisted with key intelligence — a sensitive point in US-Mexican relations, as the Trump administration has pressured President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico to be even more aggressive against drug cartels. Sheinbaum has supported increased security cooperation with the United States but firmly rejected President Trump’s proposal to deploy US forces on Mexican soil. During those weeks of quiet collaboration, officials said, Mexican authorities gave their US counterparts intelligence that helped locate Meza Flores and his family members. Whenever the weather allowed, the United States flew drone reconnaissance missions, at the request and authorization of the Mexican government, over the area where Meza Flores was believed to be. Mexican military analysts then pieced together his daily routines, intercepting his communications and studying him on live video feed from the drones, according to one of the officials. Using intercepted text messages with his mother, wife, and sister, investigators identified parties and meetings that Meza Flores — the subject of a bounty of up to $5 million from the United States for information leading to his capture — planned to attend, the official said. On Friday, Mexican special forces tracked him with intercepted radio and phone communications and drone surveillance to a home in Guasave, a city in Sinaloa, where they believed they could move in with limited collateral damage, the official said. Analysts identified Meza Flores at the house by his voice, his build, and the way he walked. An Arizona-based task force of the US Northern Command, part of the US military, also forwarded intelligence to a joint US-Mexican effort, according to a US military official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal US assessments. The operation would still have to pierce Guasave, a criminal stronghold where Meza Flores and his operatives had for decades defied Mexico’s security forces. So Mexican authorities planned diversionary raids, including one in Los Mochis, a Sinaloa city to the northwest. While that took place, more than two dozen undercover soldiers from the Mexican army’s most elite team, called the Joint Special Force, entered Guasave. As the special forces stormed into the house, dozens of other soldiers moved in to cover them, and two Mexican army Black Hawk helicopters strafed cartel gunmen — setting off a firefight that was caught on video and shared online by Guasave residents. The gunmen fired back with .50-caliber weapons mounted on armored pickup trucks. Then, with Meza Flores captured, two military helicopters flew over the house and headed toward Los Mochis as another distraction. A third hovered overhead to engage cartel gunmen. As the battle raged, special forces swept Meza Flores into an armored vehicle and out of Guasave. Meza Flores arrived in Mexico City at 5:20 a.m. Saturday aboard a military transport plane, Mexico’s Ministry of National Defense said in a statement. The ministry said seven people suspected of being cartel members were killed and eight people were arrested during the operation. The arrested included people described as high-ranking cartel operatives, such as Meza Flores’ cousin, whom Mexican authorities called his second-in-command, and a brother-in-law identified as a financial operative. Four Mexican soldiers were also killed in the operation, Mexican officials said, adding that there had been no reports so far of civilian casualties. After Meza Flores arrived in Mexico City, US officials began to disclose their part. The ambassador to Mexico, Ronald Johnson, on social media said “the exchange of strategic intelligence” had contributed to the capture. The Department of Homeland Security said the arrest followed coordination by the agency, the FBI, and Mexican authorities. On Saturday morning, US officials hailed the capture of Meza Flores as a major success in the tightening cooperation between US and Mexican security forces. In a statement, DHS called Meza Flores’ arrest “a major blow to one of Mexico’s most powerful cartel networks,” and the Drug Enforcement Administration called the arrest a “significant victory” against one of Mexico’s most violent criminal networks. “These operations demonstrate the power of global cooperation, intelligence sharing, and a unified commitment to dismantling transnational criminal organizations,” DEA head Terry Cole said on social media. Meza Flores faces federal charges in the United States of narco-terrorism, providing material support to terrorism, and engaging in a continuing criminal enterprise, the agency said. He could face life in prison or the death penalty if convicted.
